period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Opening Daadi's Letter: Reading the Spice Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.95): extract questions on Daadi's grandmother and kitchen cures.
Let us discuss (p.95): identify which spice is not useful for body pain.

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.95): fill in the blanks on methi seeds and their benefits.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to name three spices used at home, then displays or describes pictures of turmeric, clove, ginger and cardamom. Students match spice names in their own language to the English names given on p.93, building early familiarity with the text's world.

Teacher reads Daadi's letter aloud from p.93–95 at an unhurried pace while students follow in their textbooks. Teacher pauses at each spice to invite a brief student echo — repeating the spice's common name — before continuing.

Using the extract beginning 'When I was a child, I learnt them from my grandmother' (Let us read, p.95), students discuss in pairs: where did the grandmother find cures, what illness is mentioned, and what the relationship tells us about the speaker. Pairs share one response each.
Teacher poses the circling question from Let us discuss (p.95): which spice is NOT useful for body pain? Students respond by a quick show of hands; teacher confirms and closes the reading activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Daadi's letter introduces ten spices with their Hindi names alongside English names — writing both on the board as each spice comes up helps students connect the familiar to the new. A common pitfall is treating the letter as a list to memorise rather than a narrative of intergenerational knowledge; draw students' attention to how Daadi frames every remedy as something passed down from her own grandmother. Tasks on the relationship between generations (task_index 0) and the body-pain question (task_index 2) are anchored in class; the methi fill-in is set for home practice.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper: Daadi's Advice and Generations of Knowledge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.95): why did Daadi ask the children to share natural cures?
Let us think and reflect (p.95): how do natural cures pass from generation to generation?
Let us think and reflect (p.95): why should we know about healing properties of spices?

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps Daadi's letter — the spices described and the idea that knowledge came from Daadi's own grandmother — to orient students to the discussion that follows.

Teacher poses the question from Let us discuss (p.95): why did Daadi ask Vikram and Vaibhavi to share the natural cures with their friends? Students discuss in small groups and two or three groups share their reasoning with the class.

Class discussion on Let us think and reflect (p.95): how do we know that natural cures are passed from one generation to another? Teacher guides students to cite evidence from the letter — Daadi learning from her grandmother, now writing to her grandchildren.

Students respond individually in writing (2–3 sentences) to the reflective question from Let us think and reflect (p.95): why should we know about the healing properties of spices? Three or four students read their responses aloud; teacher highlights strong reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The three tasks in this sitting move from recall (Daadi's advice) through textual evidence (intergenerational transmission) to personal opinion (why healing knowledge matters) — a natural arc from comprehension to reflection. A common pitfall is students giving only one-word answers to the discussion questions; prompt them with 'What in the letter tells you that?' to keep responses anchored in the text. Task_index 4 (Daadi's final advice) is a lighter factual question and is left as a self-study pointer: students may re-read p.95 and note the answer in their own words.

periods.activity_title: Tulsi Fact Sheet and Spice Introductions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.98): complete the Tulsi fact sheet while listening to the passage.
Let us speak: choose one spice and introduce yourself as that spice to the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes or draws the blank Tulsi fact sheet on the board (p.98 format): Name, Family, First found in, Known as, Can decrease levels of, Used to treat, Used to make, How to have Tulsi leaves. Students note the eight slots they will fill.

Teacher reads the Tulsi passage (p.102) aloud slowly and clearly — once through at normal pace, then a second time with a deliberate pause after each fact. Students complete the fact sheet during the second reading. Teacher reveals answers on the board for self-correction.

Teacher demonstrates the speaking task from Let us speak: choosing one spice (e.g., turmeric) and introducing it to the class by name, part of plant, colour, texture, taste, and one benefit. Students are given a quick planning moment to choose their own spice and note three to four points.

Students take turns introducing themselves as their chosen spice — a quick paired exchange first, then four or five volunteers address the full class. Teacher offers brief, encouraging feedback after each presentation on clarity and content.

periods.teacher_notes: The Tulsi listening passage is read aloud by the teacher from the transcript (p.102); the fact sheet on p.98 provides the eight slots students must fill, so having that page open is essential. A common pitfall in the speaking activity is students reading from their notes rather than speaking naturally — remind them that a short pause to recall is fine, and model it yourself. The listening and speaking activities are complementary: Tulsi knowledge from the fact sheet can feed directly into how students describe their chosen spice's benefits.

periods.activity_title: Completing Natural Cures and Writing About Tulsi

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.99): complete the rain-washed natural cure texts using phrases from the box.
Let us write (p.100): write a short paragraph on Tulsi using the completed fact sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the writing context on p.99: Vikram's grandmother's letter was damaged by rain and some words are missing. Teacher reads both natural cures aloud — the ginger-and-honey cure and the long-pepper-basil-cardamom cure — so students hear the full shape of each text before filling blanks.

Students individually fill in the blanks for both natural cures (Let us write, p.99), choosing the correct phrases from the word box. Teacher circulates, guiding students who are uncertain by asking them to read the full sentence aloud and decide which phrase fits the meaning. Teacher reviews answers with the class.

Teacher models how to turn a fact sheet into a paragraph: writes one or two sentences on the board using the Tulsi fact sheet details — family, origin, benefits, uses. Students then draft their own short paragraph on Tulsi (Let us write, p.100), using the fact sheet they completed during the listening task.

Students swap paragraphs with a neighbour for a brief peer read: does the paragraph include at least three facts from the fact sheet? Each student makes one small revision based on their partner's response before the teacher brings the session to a close.

periods.teacher_notes: The two writing tasks in this sitting are deliberately sequenced: the guided phrase-completion (p.99) builds familiarity with the sentence structures of natural cure writing before students compose independently (p.100). A common pitfall is students copying the fact sheet verbatim without forming complete sentences for the Tulsi paragraph — encourage them to begin with a topic sentence such as 'Tulsi is a remarkable herb known as…'. Both tasks are designed to begin and end within this sitting, so peer response and any light revision happen within the available time.

periods.activity_title: Spice Properties and Modal Verbs in Action

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.96): complete the spice properties table — part of plant, colour, texture, taste.
Let us learn (p.97): match modal verbs to their functions, then complete the dialogue using four modals.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the blank spice table from Let us learn (p.96) on the board — columns: Spice, Part of plant, Colour, Texture, Taste — with rows for turmeric, fenugreek, cinnamon, clove, black pepper, cardamom. Working as a class, teacher and students complete the table by referring back to Daadi's letter on p.93–95, discussing each attribute aloud before writing.

Teacher introduces modal verbs from Let us learn (p.97) by writing six sample sentences from Daadi's letter on the board, each containing a modal (may, should, can, must, need to, used to). Students match each modal in Column A to its function in Column B individually, then the class verifies together.

Students complete the four-blank dialogue from Let us learn (p.97) using four different modals from the table — Ajay and Suman discussing Anand's illness and grandmother's natural cures. Pairs compare their choices and discuss whether a different modal would change the meaning.
Teacher invites two pairs to read their completed dialogue aloud, highlighting that different modals signal different degrees of obligation or ability — a quick consolidation before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The spice properties table (p.96) draws directly on vocabulary from Daadi's letter, so asking students to keep that page open makes the table exercise a retrieval and organisation task rather than a guessing game. A common pitfall with modal verbs is students treating them as interchangeable; the dialogue completion (p.97) is designed to expose this — when Ajay says Anand 'must' rather than 'should' rest, the degree of compulsion shifts, and discussing that shift briefly is productive. Both tasks occupy this sitting fully; no tasks are deferred.
materials: Blackboard for spice table and modal sentences

periods.activity_title: Spice Riddles: Solving, Completing and Creating

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.100): solve two riddles to identify the spices described.
Let us explore (p.100): complete the fenugreek riddle, then write an original spice riddle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads both riddles from Let us explore (p.100) aloud with expression — 'When your tummy felt funny…' and 'I come from under the ground…' — then gives students a brief paired discussion to name the spice each riddle describes. Pairs share answers and class confirms.

Teacher draws the incomplete fenugreek riddle on the board (Let us explore, p.100): 'Brownish-_____ in colour, and _____ to taste, I help everyone, to _____ their weight.' Students fill the three blanks individually, then the class agrees on the completed verse.

Students choose any spice from Daadi's letter and draft their own original riddle of four lines, using the completed riddles as models. Teacher circulates and prompts students to think about the spice's colour, texture, taste, origin, and one benefit as raw material for their lines.

Three or four students read their riddles aloud and the class guesses the spice. Teacher closes by connecting the riddle-writing activity to the way Daadi's letter itself describes each spice through its qualities — a form of playful, memorable knowledge.

periods.teacher_notes: The two solved riddles on p.100 model the form students will use for their own composition, so reading them aloud with rhythm and a pause before the answer builds the enjoyment that motivates the writing task. A common pitfall is students writing a straightforward description ('It is yellow and it is turmeric') rather than a riddle — prompt them to withhold the name and end with 'Who am I?' or 'What am I?' Task_index 2 (the sensory spice-smelling activity) requires physical spice samples and is noted here as a self-study or home extension: students may smell and feel a spice at home and describe it to a family member, without it being a class dependency.

periods.activity_title: Sensing Spices: Smell, Feel and Describe

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.100): close eyes, smell and feel spices brought to class; describe each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays four to six small portions of common spices — turmeric, cumin, cinnamon, clove, black pepper, fennel — in labelled or unlabelled containers. Students observe each sample before any activity begins, and teacher recalls briefly how Daadi described each spice's qualities in her letter.

Students close their eyes while teacher passes one spice at a time around the class for smelling and touching. After each sample, students open their eyes and jot two or three words describing the smell, texture, and any body sensation — warmth, sharpness, sweetness — without yet naming the spice.

Teacher reveals each spice's name and students compare their sensory notes with Daadi's descriptions in the letter (p.93–95) — did they detect the warmth of ginger, the sweetness of cardamom, the sharpness of black pepper? Brief whole-class discussion follows each reveal.

Students write three sentences in their exercise books connecting one chosen spice's sensory qualities to its healing benefit as described in Daadi's letter — a closing reflective consolidation that ties the hands-on experience back to the chapter's central idea.

periods.teacher_notes: This sensory activity requires the teacher to bring small quantities of four to six spices commonly available in any kitchen — turmeric, cumin, cinnamon, clove, black pepper, fennel seeds are all accessible and safe for classroom handling. A common pitfall is the activity remaining purely experiential without tying back to the text; the closing written reflection (three sentences connecting sensory quality to healing benefit) ensures students return to Daadi's letter. Students who are sensitive to strong smells may simply observe and describe visually — the activity is designed to include all learners.
materials: Small containers of four to six common spices (teacher-provided)

items.source_lo: Student reads an informational text and retrieves, interprets, and evaluates ideas using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Daadi's letter on kitchen spices, intergenerational knowledge, and natural cures for common illnesses.
items.item_stem:
In Daadi's letter, she describes how she first came to know about natural kitchen cures. Read the statements below and mark each True or False.
1. Daadi learned about kitchen cures directly from Vikram and Vaibhavi.
2. Daadi's grandmother used spices to treat weather-related illnesses.
3. Daadi advises the children to consult an elder before using any natural cure.
4. Ginger has been used in cooking for more than a thousand years according to the letter.

options.text: Daadi advises the children to consult an elder before using any natural cure.
Daadi learned about kitchen cures directly from Vikram and Vaibhavi.
Daadi's grandmother used spices to treat weather-related illnesses.
Ginger has been used in cooking for more than a thousand years according to the letter.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — Daadi learned from her own grandmother, not from the children.
2. True — the letter states Daadi's grandmother found cures for weather-related illnesses in the kitchen.
3. True — Daadi closes her letter by advising Vikram and Vaibhavi to consult an elder before using any natural cure.
4. True — the letter mentions ginger has been used in cooking for over 4000 years.

items.source_lo: Student reads an informational text and retrieves, interprets, and evaluates ideas using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Daadi's letter on kitchen spices, intergenerational knowledge, and natural cures for common illnesses.
items.item_stem: Daadi ends her letter by telling Vikram and Vaibhavi to share the natural cures with their friends. What does this tell us about Daadi's view of traditional knowledge? Support your answer with evidence from the letter.

expected_elements: Daadi believes traditional knowledge should be shared widely, not kept private.
Evidence: she herself learned from her grandmother and now teaches her grandchildren.
Sharing cures reflects the idea that traditional remedies benefit the whole community.
Students may note Daadi's instruction to consult an elder, showing respect for the tradition.

items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational passage and records specific facts accurately using listening-to-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tulsi (Holy Basil): family, origin, medicinal uses, anti-bacterial properties, Tulsi tea, and pollution protection.
items.item_stem:
The passage about Tulsi gives several specific facts about the herb. Choose the correct answer for each question.
1. According to the passage, Tulsi belongs to which plant family?
   A. Mint family   B. Basil family   C. Rose family   D. Neem family
2. Tulsi is described in the passage as:
   A. The King of Herbs   B. The Mother of Herbs   C. The Queen of Herbs   D. The Herb of Herbs
3. Which of the following is mentioned as a use of Tulsi's anti-bacterial properties?
   A. Making cooking oil   B. Making herbal hand sanitisers   C. Making pain-relief patches   D. Making fever medicine

what_each_option_reveals.Q1-A: Students who choose this may confuse Tulsi with mint, both being aromatic herbs with similar uses.
what_each_option_reveals.Q1-C: Suggests the student associated the title 'Queen of Herbs' with the rose, a common symbol of royalty.
what_each_option_reveals.Q1-D: Indicates the student may have associated Tulsi with neem, another well-known medicinal plant.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-A: Students who choose this may have misheard or misremembered 'Queen' as 'King' during listening.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-B: Suggests a reasonable but unsupported inference — the passage does not use this phrase.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-D: Indicates the student recalled the positive description but not the precise title used in the passage.
what_each_option_reveals.Q3-A: Suggests the student confused 'anti-bacterial' with cooking or food-preservation uses.
what_each_option_reveals.Q3-C: Indicates the student associated Tulsi's medicinal properties with topical pain relief, not sanitation.
what_each_option_reveals.Q3-D: Students may have over-generalised Tulsi's health benefits without attending to the specific use stated.

items.item_stem: Choose one of the following spices from Daadi's letter: turmeric, cumin, black pepper, or cardamom. Introduce yourself to the class as that spice. In your introduction, tell the class: your name (English and Hindi), which part of the plant you come from, your colour and texture, your taste, and one healing benefit Daadi mentions in her letter.

expected_elements: Names the spice in both English and Hindi correctly.
Correctly states the plant part (e.g., root, seed, bark).

items.item_stem: Daadi's letter describes how natural kitchen spices have been trusted for generations as home remedies. Do you think young people today should learn about these traditional remedies, or is it enough to rely on modern medicine? Give your opinion and support it with at least one example from Daadi's letter.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion on traditional versus modern medicine.
Supports opinion with at least one spice example from the letter.
Acknowledges Daadi's advice to consult an elder as a responsible practice.
Speaks in complete sentences with adequate volume and clarity.

items.source_lo: Student completes and composes functional informational writing using guided and independent writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Natural cures for cough (ginger-honey; long-pepper-basil-cardamom-honey) and a paragraph on Tulsi from the fact sheet.
items.item_stem:
A friend has written instructions for a simple home remedy using ginger and honey to treat a cough, but has left some steps incomplete. Complete the instructions below by filling in each blank with a suitable word or phrase so that the remedy makes sense as a set of clear directions.

Natural cure for cough:
Step 1: Take _______ piece of fresh ginger and wash it carefully.
Step 2: Grate the ginger finely and squeeze out _______ into a small bowl.
Step 3: Add a small _______ of honey to the ginger juice and stir well.
Step 4: _______ the mixture twice a day to help soothe a cough.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable answers: Step 1: a small / one; Step 2: the juice; Step 3: amount / spoonful; Step 4: Take / Drink / Have. Accept any clear, logical phrase that makes the instruction complete and coherent.

items.source_context: Natural cures for cough (ginger-honey; long-pepper-basil-cardamom-honey) and a paragraph on Tulsi from the fact sheet.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are writing a short entry for a school health magazine. Write a paragraph of five to seven sentences about Tulsi (Holy Basil) as a healing herb. Your paragraph should include: where Tulsi is found, at least two medicinal uses, one way to consume it, and why it is called 'the Queen of Herbs'. Write in your own words.

expected_elements: States where Tulsi is found (north central India, now across India).
Mentions at least two medicinal uses (e.g., blood sugar, digestion, anti-bacterial).
Describes one way to consume it (raw leaves or Tulsi tea).
Explains or implies why it is called 'the Queen of Herbs'.
Written in clear, connected sentences appropriate for a magazine audience.

items.source_context: Spice attribute vocabulary (part of plant, texture, taste) and modal verbs (may, should, can, must, need to, used to) from Daadi's letter.
items.item_stem: Match each modal verb in Column A with its correct function in Column B. The modals are the same ones Daadi uses in her letter to Vikram and Vaibhavi.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (Modal verb) | Column B (Function) |
|---|---|
| may | ability |
| should | necessity |
| can | suggestion |
| must | past habit |
| need to | permission or possibility |
| used to | compulsion |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: may — permission or possibility; should — suggestion; can — ability; must — compulsion; need to — necessity; used to — past habit.

items.source_context: Spice attribute vocabulary (part of plant, texture, taste) and modal verbs (may, should, can, must, need to, used to) from Daadi's letter.
items.item_stem:
Read the following conversation between two students discussing Daadi's letter. Choose the most appropriate modal verb from the brackets to complete each sentence. Use each modal only once.

Rhea: Have you read Daadi's letter about spices? She says ginger (1. can / must) cure colds.
Sameer: Yes! She also says we (2. should / used to) try natural remedies before going to the doctor.
Rhea: My grandmother (3. used to / need to) make turmeric milk every winter for us.
Sameer: My mother says I (4. must / may) drink it every morning during the cold season — no excuses!

Write the word you have chosen for each blank.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. can (ability — ginger is able to cure colds); 2. should (suggestion — advising to try natural remedies); 3. used to (past habit — grandmother made it regularly in the past); 4. must (compulsion — no choice allowed). Accept 'may' for blank 1 only if the student provides a brief justification about possibility rather than certainty.

items.source_context: Spice riddles — solving, completing the fenugreek riddle, writing an original riddle, and sensory exploration of spices.
items.item_stem:
Read the riddle below and answer the questions that follow.

'I come from under the ground,
Thousands of years, I've been around.
For cooking you use me daily,
From cold I can cure you surely.'

(a) Which spice does this riddle describe? Give one reason from the riddle to support your answer.
(b) The riddle says this spice can cure you 'from cold'. Which detail from Daadi's letter supports this claim?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) Ginger (adrak). The clue 'I come from under the ground' points to a root, and ginger is a root used daily in cooking for over 4000 years. (b) Daadi's letter states that ginger helps with cough, cold, and pain.

items.source_lo: Student extends textual knowledge through creative problem-solving and original composition using hands-on extension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Spice riddles — solving, completing the fenugreek riddle, writing an original riddle, and sensory exploration of spices.
items.item_stem: Write your own riddle of four lines about one of the spices described in Daadi's letter (you may choose turmeric, cumin, cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, or clove). Your riddle should: hint at the spice's colour or texture, mention the part of the plant it comes from, refer to one healing benefit from the letter, and end with the question 'Who am I?' Do not name the spice anywhere in the riddle.

expected_elements: Four lines that read as a coherent riddle in verse or near-verse form.
At least one accurate sensory clue (colour, texture, or plant part) from the chapter.
One healing benefit drawn from Daadi's letter, embedded naturally in the lines.
Ends with 'Who am I?' and does not name the spice anywhere.
